summary:
The Cayman Islands' constitutional discrimination grounds were drafted in 2009 without sexual-orientation protection. The omission drew criticism from the United Kingdom parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, which called it deplorable and warned that Cayman courts could afford less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires; the Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the list of grounds was open-ended. No enumerated constitutional ground anchors a discrimination claim, and no trans-specific ground is listed.

No domestic route to marriage exists. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban. Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration: in December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, an overseas marriage therefore carries immigration effects even though the territory offers no domestic route to marry.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, among them the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation.

No trans-specific legal provision is documented for the Cayman Islands. Nothing in the available sources addresses gender recognition, identity documents, single-sex facilities, healthcare access or hate-crime protection, and no trans-specific incident or enforcement action is recorded.
tangentialFactors:
Public expression is arranged rather than free-standing. Organisers of the 2021 Pride parade asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection as a condition of the public-space route, so the broad official participation came with negotiated limits on visible intimacy.

Partner recognition rests on an immigration decision and an appellate equality holding rather than on a marriage statute: the statutory ban on same-sex marriage was restored on appeal in August 2019, while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived. The protection therefore sits in administrative practice and case law rather than in legislation.

The 2009 constitutional drafting episode is the clearest documented instance of the administering power and the territory disagreeing in public over LGBT protections, with the Foreign Affairs Committee invoking the European Convention on Human Rights as an external benchmark the local framework might not meet.
localsOnly:
Residents have no domestic route to marry. The Grand Court struck the statutory ban down in March 2019 and the Court of Appeal restored it in August 2019, so a couple must marry abroad for the marriage to have any local effect.

Where they do, immigration authorities recognise the overseas marriage. The December 2020 recognition of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder's Irish marriage, resting on the appellate holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds, gives couples an immigration route that the marriage statute does not provide.

The constitution's discrimination grounds do not expressly cover sexual orientation, so residents have no enumerated constitutional ground on which to challenge discriminatory treatment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific legal provision for the Cayman Islands appears in the available sources. Gender-recognition procedures, identity-document and marker rules, single-sex facilities, healthcare access and hate-crime provisions are all unsourced, and no trans-specific incident or enforcement action is recorded.

The final text of the 2009 constitution, and whether the open-ended list of discrimination grounds has since been read to cover gender identity, is unresolved.

Whether the condition organisers placed on displays of affection at the 2021 Pride parade was enforced, and by whom, is not sourced.
